content: TLUD (Top-Lit UpDraft) pyrolysis for fine branches and ramilles (<10 cm): operation at 450-550 C produces agricultural biochar for acidic ferrallitic soils (Gabonese soils typically pH 4.5-5.5; biochar application 1-5 t/ha raises pH and CEC). Refillable batch stove, primary air from below, secondary air above the fuel bed; residence 2-4 hours. Carbon retention ~35-50% of feedstock carbon; CO2-equivalent benefit when biochar is soil-applied is permanent sequestration. Ecological cooking briquettes: charcoal fines + 5% cassava starch binder, extruded and dried to 12-14% moisture; calorific value 22-26 MJ/kg. TLUD emission factor is 80-90% lower than open-air burning for PM2.5. Residue_type: branches. Technology: tlud_pyrolysis.

Stump and thick-root valorization for luxury artisan furniture and sculpture: harvest stumps after felling with minimal soil disturbance; natural air-drying under shade for 12-18 months down to 12% moisture content stabilizes unique grain burls and interlocked roots, preventing checking and warping. Oak/okoume burl figure (moire) commands premium prices; a single large Moabi or Okoume burl can yield 3-8 furniture blanks (stool tops, veneer blocks). End-grain sealer (PVA or latex) applied immediately after felling. Species targets: Baillonella toxisperma, Aucoumea klaineana. Residue_type: stumps, roots. Technology: air_drying_burl_craft. Root extract bio-pesticide: macerate fine roots, solvent water 80 C, filter; ecologically relevant for local agroforestry.

Bark hot-water tannin extraction for formaldehyde-free bio-glues: chip bark, extract at 80-90 C with 2% sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) for 45-60 minutes; tannin yield 20-35% of dry bark weight for Pterocarpus soyauxii and Aucoumea klaineana. Condense tannin extract with sucrose or glyoxal crosslinker instead of formaldehyde; plywood panels meet E0/E1 emission class. Bark mass rule: 10-14% of commercial trunk volume; a 60 cm DBH Okoume (volume trunk ~1.2 m3) yields ~0.12-0.17 m3 bark, roughly 40-70 kg dry bark, 8-24 kg tannin extract. Residue_type: bark. Technology: hotwater_tannin. Industrial use case: local plywood mill bio-adhesive, disposes of bark piles that otherwise ferment and emit methane.

Mycelium bio-board from sawdust and foliage: pasteurize raw sawdust at 60-70 C for 60 minutes to kill competitors; inoculate with local Ganoderma or Pleurotus (oyster mushroom) spawn at 5-10% inoculation rate; incubate 14-21 days at 24-26 C in dark, humidity 70-95%, until white mycelium colonizes the substrate; then kiln-dry at 60-80 C for 12-24 hours to deactivate growth. Resulting structural panels: density 120-250 kg/m3, compressive strength suitable for insulation and non-load-bearing panels; fully compostable at end of life. Dual benefit: Pleurotus flushes (2-3 harvests) before board formation provide protein income. Residue_type: sawdust, foliage. Technology: mycelium_board.

Thick branches (>15 cm) mobile sawing: portable band mill or chainsaw mill with 5 mm kerf converts thick branch wood into dimension lumber or craft boards; recovery 45-60% of gross volume (accounting for kerf losses of 5 mm per cut). Branch wood of Azobe (Lophira alata) has exceptional hardness suitable for tool handles and flooring offcuts. Logistics: co-locate milling at landing sites to avoid transporting low-volume residues; chipper residue from edging feeds TLUD. Residue_type: branches. Technology: mobile_sawing. Waste minimization: every branch routed to milling or TLUD reduces open-air pile decomposition (methane) — see carbon offset metadata.

NTFP kernel oil pressing (Andok / Irvingia gabonensis, Njansang / Ricinodendron heudelotii): sun-dry or kiln-dry kernels to 6-8% moisture, crack the shell, grind to a paste and press with a manual or motorized screw press. Cold pressing yields 40-55% oil by kernel weight; dika fat (Irvingia) is rich in myristic and lauric acids and is a premium cosmetic/soap input, while njansang oil is used in varnish and skincare. The press cake (45-55% of kernel mass) is protein-rich and is used as animal feed or composted. Community business model: a women-led cooperative with one screw press (2-5 t kernels/season) can produce oleaginous extracts and cosmetics; peels and press cake residues feed TLUD pyrolysis or compost. Energy input low (manual press); the highest-value residue stream in a concession-adjacent NTFP supply chain. Residue_type: mixed. Technology: ntfp_oil_press.

Sawdust densification into fuel pellets and briquettes: dry sawdust and planer shavings to 10-12% moisture, mill to a uniform 3-5 mm particle size, then densify in a pellet press (or briquette extruder) at 90-120 C and 100-150 MPa without external binder (lignin plasticises). Pellet calorific value 16-18 MJ/kg at 8% moisture; durability index > 95% (ISO 17225-2 grade). Screen oversize and fines (< 5%) are recirculated, keeping residual waste near zero. Compared with open-air decomposition of moist residue piles, pelletizing avoids methane emissions and displaces charcoal, reducing household PM2.5. Business case: the Owendo/Port-Gentil energy-briquette cooperatives convert sawmill fines into a storable, exportable solid fuel. Residue_type: sawdust. Technology: sawdust_pelletizing.

Foliage and fine-ramille composting and fodder: crown foliage and twigs < 10 cm are chipped (2-5 cm) and either (a) composted in windrows - C:N adjusted with bark/N-rich material, turned every 5-7 days, 6-8 weeks to mature compost for nurseries and community gardens on acidic ferrallitic soils - or (b) used as livestock browse for small ruminants after wilting, noting that some species (e.g. high-tannin Pterocarpus) should be limited. Foliar biomass carries the highest nutrient concentration of all residue streams (N 1-3% dry mass); composting it returns limiting phosphorus and base cations to soils. Leachate from windrows is captured as liquid fertiliser. Where foliage is abundant, partial gasification in a TLUD after drying converts it to biochar as an alternative. Residue_type: foliage. Technology: foliage_compost_fodder.
